api/generated/SmartDock.DockManager.html.summary: Class DockManager Namespace SmartDock Assembly SmartDock.dll Hosts a DockLayout. Register content by id, assign Layout, and the control builds the splits, tabs, floating windows, and auto-hide bars. Only the selected tab's content is in the tree. Drag a tab along its strip to reorder it, or off the strip to float it, then drop it on a guide to dock it. A tool, or a float of tools, can also drop on an auto-hide strip. Guides and the landing preview are drawn in a topmost overlay so the dragged window cannot cover them. Another float under the pointer shows that float's compass and edge guides; the topmost one wins, and the dragged window is skipped. A dock guide or that float wins where it overlaps an auto-hide hot zone. Documents are not an auto-hide target. The same gesture is covered by the internal drag methods, which call DockDragSession with coordinates and no mouse. Ctrl+Tab switches panes. DockCommands closes, cycles document tabs, toggles float and auto-hide, and saves the layout. When AnimationsEnabled is set and Windows animations are on, reordered tab headers slide and the dock guides fade. The auto-hide flyout is a child window so it paints above an HwndHost pane. A click or focus inside that hosted window, including a child of it, activates the pane and leaves the click with the native window. The flyout opens and closes at its arranged size: a render transform does not move that HWND. Those clocks do not change layout, focus, or events. ResizeGripThickness is the hit zone of a splitter, a flyout edge, and a float's border. ResizeMode applies splitter, flyout, and floating-window sizes live, once per frame, or as a preview on release. public sealed class DockManager : Border, IAnimatable, ISupportInitialize, Chrome, floats, guides, the switcher, menus, and the toolbar dialogs paint with resource keys, so Apply(FrameworkElement, DockThemeKind) can replace those brushes and open windows repaint. CreateMenuResources() is the opt-in menu and context menu. Nothing merges it on its own. CreateScrollBarResources() is the scrollbar, tooltip, and focus visual. The dock manager, each float, the switcher, and the toolbar dialogs merge it themselves. A host merges another copy for bars outside the dock. DockToolBar Attached properties for a ToolBar placed in ToolBars. A toolbar created from ToolBarsSource reads the same values from DockToolBarItem instead. KeyProperty identifies one button. DockToolBarCaption Caption of a floating toolbar. PART_Grip drags and double-clicks to dock when visible; when the title is hidden, the grip collapses and the caption outside PART_Close is the drag handle. PART_Close hides the toolbar. PART_Title shows Title and trims it when the window is narrow. A trimmed title gets a tooltip with the full text. A vertical float hides the title and keeps that tooltip, because the button column is too narrow for it. A custom toolbar name is not drawn here; it is the tooltip. The close button is 22 DIP on a horizontal caption. On a vertical one it is a 32/3 DIP box (about 10.7) and its glyph is two thirds of the template's size, so a narrow column keeps a drag area beside it. DockToolBarCustomize Chevron that opens the Add or Remove Buttons menu. The default template strokes Dock.Text. DockToolBarDrop The line drawn while a toolbar is dragged over a band or an edge. The default template fills Dock.Accent. The control does not take the pointer. DockToolBarGrip The grip drawn at the leading edge of a toolbar. Drag it to move the toolbar. Leaving the tray undocks it into a floating window while the button is still held. Double-click docks a floating toolbar back to the band it left. The default template paints three dots with Dock.Muted on Dock.Chrome. DockToolBarItem Bindable properties for one toolbar in ToolBarsSource. A Style assigned to ToolBarItemStyle targets this type. Its setters bind against the item, which is the DataContext. The manager reads these values when the toolbar enters the source and again when they change. This element is not placed in the visual tree. DockToolBarTray One edge of the dock that hosts toolbar bands. The template's PART_Bands panel receives one child per band. The default template fills Dock.Chrome. DockTree Short constructors for a layout tree. The same tree can be built with object initializers or XAML. DragPointer Reused pointer state for DockDragSession. Fill Leaves and Headers in place so a drag move does not allocate those lists. FloatWindow A floating window. Coordinates are device-independent pixels. HiddenEntry A pane Hide(DockLayout, string) took out of the tree, plus the place Show(DockLayout, string) returns it to. Default place fields are omitted from JSON. LayoutMap Resolves a layout to content ids. Pass the ids the application can create and the map reports which saved panes have no factory (MissingContentIds) and which factories the layout does not use (UnplacedContentIds). Both of those lists are sorted. Panels follows the visible tree: main, then floating windows, then auto-hide edges. Hidden panes are not listed. A known id that is only hidden is not unplaced. An unknown hidden id is missing. SplitChild One cell of a SplitNode. SplitNode A resizable split. Proportions are positive weights, not required to sum to 1. TabGroupNode A tabbed group of panes. The selected index is part of the saved layout. TabStrip Header geometry for a tab strip, in the same coordinates as the pointer. ToolBarBands Hit testing and placement for toolbar bands. The host measures the trays and passes the rectangles. Hit(DockRect, string, ReadOnlySpan<ToolBarBarRect>, ReadOnlySpan<ToolBarBandRect>, ReadOnlySpan<ToolBarTrayRect>, double, double, string, string) does not allocate. ToolBarCustomizationEventArgs The toolbar and button a customization change refers to. ToolBarDrag Along-axis offsets that open a gap while a toolbar button is dragged. ToolBarEntry Where one toolbar sits. Edge, Band, Index, and Offset stay the last docked place while Floating is set, so a double-click can put it back. PaneId names the pane that hosts it. Both null is the main window. WindowId is an old floating-window edge; the dock moves that toolbar to the main window's top tray. Default values are omitted from JSON. ToolBarItemEntry One customized button. Key is the host's item key. HomeId is the toolbar whose collection owns the item; null means BarId. Items with no entry stay in collection order on their own toolbar. ToolBarItems Ordering and visibility overlay for toolbar buttons. The host collection is not modified. An item with no entry stays on its own toolbar. A new item is inserted after the nearest preceding collection neighbor that is still on that toolbar. Unknown keys are ignored. ToolBarLayout Toolbar bands and button customization stored with a DockLayout. Null on the layout, and omitted from JSON, when the host has no toolbar state. A document written before toolbars existed has no toolBars object and still loads. WorkAreas Places a floating window that lies entirely outside every monitor onto the nearest work area. A window that intersects any work area is left where it is. Coordinates are device-independent pixels, the same space as FloatWindow bounds. Structs AutoHideHit An auto-hide drop. Preview is the strip, or the hot zone when the strip is collapsed. AutoHideStrip One auto-hide strip in the same coordinates as the pointer. Collapsed is an empty strip: the hit test uses HotZoneOf(DockRect, AutoHideEdge) instead of Bounds. DockEditResult Result of a layout edit. Refusals such as "cannot close" do not throw. DockPaneStateChange One pane whose DockPaneState differs between two layouts. DockRect A rectangle in the same coordinate space the host uses for pointer positions. DockTarget A window that can receive a dock drop. WindowId is empty for the main host. A larger ZOrder is painted above a smaller one. RootId is the node edge guides dock against. DragStep What a drag update did to the layout. Structure changes need a view rebuild; a follow only moves a window. TabsMoved means the dragged tab changed slots. The host redraws that strip and does not publish yet. DropGuide A dock target. Root-edge buttons dock against the whole host; other buttons dock against one leaf. NodeBounds Bounds of a leaf tab group, supplied by the view. PaneLocation Where a pane currently lives. Group is null for auto-hidden panes. PlacedPanel A pane located by Build(DockLayout, ISet<string>?) so a host can reattach content by ContentId. ScreenDip A point in device-independent pixels (1/96 inch), the units stored on a FloatWindow. TabStrip.Header One header along the strip. Index is the pane's index in its group. A negative index means this list is the whole group in order, and the list position is the model index. TabStrip.Range Contiguous headers that fit in a strip. First is the model index of the leftmost one. Overflow is true when at least one header is hidden. ToolBarBandRect Arranged bounds of one band. Bands on an edge are passed in band order. ToolBarBarRect Arranged bounds of one docked toolbar, in the same coordinates as the pointer. PaneId and WindowId are empty for a main-window tray. ToolBarDrop A drop target. Float tears the toolbar off. InsertBand opens a new band and shifts bands at Band and after it. Indicator is the line to draw. ToolBarFloatMember One toolbar inside a floating window, in the same coordinates as the pointer. Members of one window are visited in Index order by TryHitFloat(ReadOnlySpan<ToolBarFloatWindow>, ReadOnlySpan<ToolBarFloatMember>, string, string, double, double, out string, out int, out DockRect). ToolBarFloatWindow One floating toolbar window. Id is FloatId, or the toolbar id when the window holds one toolbar. A larger ZOrder is painted above a smaller one. Vertical stacks members top to bottom. ToolBarGridFit One snapped size of a floating toolbar. Columns and Rows place every button. Horizontal fills a row and then the next. Vertical fills a column and then the next. Width and Height are the window: the cells plus the chrome given to FitGrid(int, double, double, double, double, double, double, double, double, double, double, int), and at least that orientation's minimum width. Vertical is false when Width is at least Height, including a square. ToolBarItemRef An item as the host collection currently holds it. ToolBarPackItem One toolbar to place in a band. Offset and Size are along the band. ToolBarSite One place a toolbar can dock. An empty PaneId and WindowId is the main window. A pane id is that pane's content. A window id is a floating window's id. A window with a larger ZOrder is painted above one with a smaller value. OwnerId is the window that shows a pane: empty for the main window, else a floating window's id. ToolBarSlot One slot in a toolbar after the customization overlay is applied. Hidden slots stay in the list. ToolBarTrayRect Arranged bounds of one edge tray. Enums AutoHideEdge Edge of the dock root that holds auto-hidden panes. DockCaptionRole Which caption this bar is. The default template hides the title row on a strip caption. DockGesturePhase Where a DockDragSession is in its gesture. DockKind Document panes live in the document well. Tool panes are tool windows and may auto-hide. DockPaneState Whether a pane is in the main tree, a floating window, an auto-hide strip, or hidden. The first three match PanelPlacement. Hidden is a pane kept in Hidden, which is not a placement the host shows. DockResizeHit Which edge of a floating window a pointer is on. None is the client area. DockResizeMode Whether a splitter, a flyout edge, or a floating window resizes during the drag or on release. DockSide Where a pane is docked relative to an anchor node. DockThemeKind Dark, light, or blue dock chrome. Dark is the default. PanelPlacement Where a pane sits after a layout is applied. SplitOrientation Children of a horizontal split sit left to right. A vertical split stacks them top to bottom. TabPlacement Which edge of a tab group draws the tab strip. ToolBarAlignment Which end of a band a toolbar packs against. Start is the left of a horizontal band and the top of a vertical one. End is the right of a horizontal band and the bottom of a vertical one. Start is the default and is omitted from JSON. ToolBarCustomizationChange What changed in a toolbar or in its buttons. ToolBarEdge Which edge of the dock hosts a toolbar band. A floating toolbar keeps the edge it left.

api/index.html.title: API reference | SmartDock
api/index.html.summary: API reference These pages are generated from the XML comments in the SmartDock and SmartDock.Core assemblies. Both use the SmartDock namespace. SmartDock.Core has the layout tree, DockEdit, DockSerializer, dock-guide hit testing, and the toolbar layout records. It doesn't reference WPF. SmartDock has DockManager, DockCommands, DockTheme, and the chrome controls such as DockTabHeader, DockCaption, DockDropPreview, and DockGuideButton. For how-to guides, start with the articles: Getting started Layout Saving and loading layouts Toolbars Keyboard Themes Events and callbacks

articles/events.html.title: Events and callbacks | SmartDock
articles/events.html.summary: Events and callbacks All events are on DockManager. This handler set cancels closing the "readme" pane and records the rest: public static string? Last { get; private set; } public static void Watch(DockManager dock) { dock.PaneClosing += (_, e) => { if (e.ContentId == "readme") e.Cancel = true; }; dock.PaneClosed += (_, e) => Last = e.ContentId; dock.PaneStateChanged += (_, e) => Last = e.NewState.ToString(); dock.ActivePaneChanged += (_, e) => Last = e.NewContentId; dock.PaneMounted += (_, e) => Last = e.ContentId; dock.PaneUnmounted += (_, e) => Last = e.ContentId; dock.LayoutChanged += (_, _) => Last = "layout"; dock.ToolBarCustomizationChanged += (_, e) => Last = e.ToolBarId; } LayoutChanged Fires after a structural edit, a tab selection change, or a splitter move. Use it to know when to save. Reordering a tab by dragging fires it once, on release. Tearing a pane off into a float fires it as soon as the pane leaves its group. Moving a floating window does not fire it, and neither does a close that a PaneClosing handler cancelled. PaneClosing and PaneClosed PaneClosing fires before a pane is removed, with ContentId and Cancel. Set Cancel to keep the pane; the layout stays as it was and LayoutChanged does not fire. This is where you ask about unsaved changes. It fires for the tab close button, the flyout close button, ClosePane (and so Ctrl+F4), and for a floating window's close button, Alt+F4, or Window.Close. Closing a floating window fires it once for each pane that can close; if any handler cancels, the window stays open and nothing closes. Panes in that window that can't close are docked back without the event, unless they have HideOnClose. A pane with HideOnClose still gets PaneClosing from the same buttons and from ClosePane, but is then hidden rather than removed, so PaneClosed does not fire. PaneClosed fires after a user close has removed the pane. It does not fire when Layout is replaced (including LoadLayout and a SavedLayout change that loads), or for RemovePane, HidePane, ShowPane, or EditLayout; those report PaneStateChanged instead. Closing the host window doesn't fire PaneClosing; it only dismisses the floating windows. PaneStateChanged Fires when a pane moves between Docked, Floating, AutoHidden, and Hidden, with ContentId, OldState, and NewState. Replacing Layout fires it for every pane whose state changed. The state says where the pane is in the layout, not whether its content is on screen. A docked pane in an unselected tab, an auto-hidden pane with its flyout closed, or a float that hasn't placed its content yet has no content in a host. Use PaneMounted and PaneUnmounted for that. ActivePaneChanged Fires when ActiveContentId changes. OldContentId or NewContentId is null when there was, or is, no active pane. The active pane is the one whose tab was selected last, whose content last got keyboard focus, or that last received a click or focus inside hosted native content. The bright accent follows that pane: its selected tab, or its lone caption, draws Dock.Accent. The selected tab or lone caption of every other pane draws Dock.AccentInactive. The same rule covers a docked group, a floating window, and an open auto-hide flyout. A click in an HwndHost, including a child of that window, activates the pane that hosts it. The click is not taken from the native window, and focus stays there. To activate a pane from code, call ActivatePane. It selects the tab of a docked or floating pane, opens an auto-hidden pane's flyout, and shows a hidden pane first. An unknown id does nothing. SelectPane selects a tab and makes that pane active without moving keyboard focus, so an open flyout stays open. PaneMounted and PaneUnmounted PaneMounted fires after a pane's content element has been put in a host: the selected tab of a docked group, a floating window, or an open flyout. PaneUnmounted fires after it has been taken out again. The two always alternate for a given content id. Moving content to a different host fires PaneUnmounted, then PaneMounted. If the element stays in the same parent, neither fires, so changing a title or icon doesn't. A selected pane stays mounted as long as its group's view is kept. ToolBarCustomizationChanged Fires after a toolbar button is reordered, moved, hidden, shown, or reset, and when a toolbar is shown or hidden. See Toolbars.

articles/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | SmartDock
articles/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started You need three things: a DockManager in a window, a factory for each content id, and a layout. The manager calls a factory the first time its pane is shown and keeps the control, so moving, floating, or reloading the pane reuses the same instance. Register factories before you assign Layout. A pane shown without a factory gets a "Missing content: id" placeholder, and that placeholder stays cached while the pane is in the layout. The manager starts with no layout, so assign one before the window is shown, or the first frame is empty. <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.GettingStartedWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <dock:DockManager x:Name="Dock" /> </Window> using System.Windows; using System.Windows.Controls; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public partial class GettingStartedWindow : Window { public GettingStartedWindow() { InitializeComponent(); Dock.RegisterContent("solution", () => new TreeView()); Dock.RegisterContent("program", () => new TextBox()); Dock.RegisterContent("readme", () => new TextBox()); Dock.Layout = DockTree.Create(DockTree.Split("root", SplitOrientation.Horizontal, DockTree.Weighted(0.25, DockTree.Tabs("tools", DockKind.Tool, DockTree.Tool("solution", "Solution Explorer", canClose: false))), DockTree.Weighted(0.75, DockTree.Tabs("docs", DockKind.Document, DockTree.Document("program", "Program.cs"), DockTree.Document("readme", "README.md"))))); } } A horizontal DockTree.Split lays out its children left to right, a vertical one top to bottom. DockTree.Weighted gives a child its weight. DockTree.Tool creates a tool pane that can auto-hide; DockTree.Document creates a document pane that can't. Content ids are case-sensitive and must be unique within a layout. Use the same string in the layout and in RegisterContent. The WPF package pulls in SmartDock.Core. If a project only builds or stores layouts and never shows a window, reference SmartDock.Core alone and use DockTree and DockSerializer from there. Both packages use the SmartDock namespace. Next: Layout and Saving and loading layouts.

articles/keyboard.html.title: Keyboard | SmartDock
articles/keyboard.html.summary: Keyboard Ctrl+Tab Hold Ctrl and press Tab to open the pane switcher. It lists the visible panes, most recently activated first; hidden panes are left out and tools are marked "Tool". With fewer than two panes the key does nothing. The host window and every floating window listen for the key, so it works even when focus is outside the panes. The popup opens over the window that got the key and stays there while you move through the list. The first press highlights the previous pane. Tab or Down moves down the list, Shift+Tab or Up moves back, and the list wraps. Release Ctrl to activate the highlighted pane: its tab is selected, an auto-hidden pane's flyout opens, and a floating pane's window comes to the front. Escape closes the switcher without changing the active pane. The activation order lives in memory only. It is not saved with the layout. Commands DockCommands has routed commands that DockManager already handles. Their default keys are in each command's InputGestures, which is read on every key press, so a change takes effect immediately. Command Default key What it does ClosePane Ctrl+F4 Closes the active pane. A pane with HideOnClose is hidden instead of removed. NextDocument Ctrl+PageDown Activates the next document tab. PreviousDocument Ctrl+PageUp Activates the previous document tab. ToggleFloat none Floats the active pane, or docks a floating pane back. ToggleAutoHide none Auto-hides the active tool, or pins a tool that is already on an auto-hide strip. SaveLayout none Writes the current layout into SavedLayout. Does nothing when no layout is assigned. LoadLayout none Loads SavedLayout again. Does nothing when that string is null or empty. A non-empty command parameter is loaded instead, then stored in SavedLayout. public static void Run(DockManager dock) { DockCommands.ClosePane.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.NextDocument.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.PreviousDocument.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.ToggleFloat.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.ToggleAutoHide.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.SaveLayout.Execute(null, dock); DockCommands.LoadLayout.Execute(null, dock); } ToggleFloat opens the float at (80, 80), 480 by 360, if the pane is allowed to float, and docks a pane that is already floating back. ToggleAutoHide does nothing when the active pane can't auto-hide. To rebind a command, replace its gestures: public static void RebindClose() { DockCommands.ClosePane.InputGestures.Clear(); DockCommands.ClosePane.InputGestures.Add(new KeyGesture(Key.W, ModifierKeys.Control)); } DockCommands is static, so this changes the key for every DockManager in the process.

articles/layout.html.title: Layout | SmartDock
articles/layout.html.summary: Layout A DockLayout holds the main tree, the floating windows, four auto-hide strips, and any hidden panes. You change it with DockEdit. Each call returns a DockEditResult instead of throwing: a refused edit leaves the tree as it was, and a tree produced by a successful structural edit is valid to save. Splits and tabs You can build the tree in code or declare it in XAML. In XAML you need two prefixes: the controls live in the SmartDock assembly and the model types in SmartDock.Core, both under the SmartDock namespace. Factories still have to be registered before Layout is set. DockManager is sealed, so you can't do that in a subclass constructor. This sample uses an attached property instead: XAML applies attributes on the start tag before property elements, so Prepare runs before the Layout element is assigned. using System.Windows; using System.Windows.Controls; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public static class SampleContent { public static readonly DependencyProperty PrepareProperty = DependencyProperty.RegisterAttached( "Prepare", typeof(bool), typeof(SampleContent), new PropertyMetadata(false, OnPrepare)); public static void SetPrepare(DependencyObject element, bool value) => element.SetValue(PrepareProperty, value); public static bool GetPrepare(DependencyObject element) => (bool)element.GetValue(PrepareProperty); private static void OnPrepare(DependencyObject element, DependencyPropertyChangedEventArgs args) { if (element is not DockManager dock || args.NewValue is not true) return; dock.RegisterContent("solution", () => new TreeView()); dock.RegisterContent("properties", () => new TextBox()); dock.RegisterContent("program", () => new TextBox()); dock.RegisterContent("readme", () => new TextBox()); } } <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.LayoutWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" xmlns:local="clr-namespace:SmartDock.Docs.Samples" xmlns:model="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock.Core" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <dock:DockManager local:SampleContent.Prepare="True"> <dock:DockManager.Layout> <model:DockLayout> <model:DockLayout.Root> <model:SplitNode Id="root" Orientation="Horizontal"> <model:SplitNode.Children> <model:SplitChild Proportion="0.25"> <model:SplitChild.Node> <model:TabGroupNode Id="tools" Kind="Tool"> <model:TabGroupNode.Panels> <model:DockPane ContentId="solution" Title="Solution Explorer" Kind="Tool" CanClose="False" CanAutoHide="True" /> <model:DockPane ContentId="properties" Title="Properties" Kind="Tool" /> </model:TabGroupNode.Panels> </model:TabGroupNode> </model:SplitChild.Node> </model:SplitChild> <model:SplitChild Proportion="0.75"> <model:SplitChild.Node> <model:TabGroupNode Id="docs" Kind="Document"> <model:TabGroupNode.Panels> <model:DockPane ContentId="program" Title="Program.cs" /> <model:DockPane ContentId="readme" Title="README.md" /> </model:TabGroupNode.Panels> </model:TabGroupNode> </model:SplitChild.Node> </model:SplitChild> </model:SplitNode.Children> </model:SplitNode> </model:DockLayout.Root> </model:DockLayout> </dock:DockManager.Layout> </dock:DockManager> </Window> Proportion is a positive weight. The weights don't need to add up to 1. A tool pane can auto-hide only when CanAutoHide is true. DockTree.Tool sets it for you, but a DockPane declared in XAML leaves it false unless you set it. TabGroupNode.SelectedIndex is the selected tab, and it is saved with the layout. DockManager.TabPlacement (tool groups) and DocumentTabPlacement (document groups) put the tab strip above or below the content. Both default to Top. The same tree in code: public static DockLayout Build() { return DockTree.Create(DockTree.Split("root", SplitOrientation.Horizontal, DockTree.Weighted(0.25, DockTree.Tabs("tools", DockKind.Tool, DockTree.Tool("solution", "Solution Explorer", canClose: false), DockTree.Tool("properties", "Properties"))), DockTree.Weighted(0.75, DockTree.Tabs("docs", DockKind.Document, DockTree.Document("program", "Program.cs"), DockTree.Document("readme", "README.md"))))); } Docking DockEdit.Dock moves a pane that is already in the layout. DockSide.Left, Right, Top, and Bottom split the anchor and give the pane DockEdit.DefaultProportion (0.25) unless you pass another weight. DockSide.Center adds the pane as a tab, so the anchor has to be a tab group. On a live manager, call DockManager.DockPaneTo. It runs the same edit and raises LayoutChanged if the tree changed. Floating windows DockEdit.Float takes a pane out of the tree and puts it in a new floating window at the bounds you pass, in device-independent pixels. DockEdit.DockBack puts it back: into the tab group it came from if that group still exists, otherwise into the first main-tree group of the same kind, otherwise into a new group on the right. A floating window can be saved maximized. Its x, y, width, and height are then the restored bounds, not the maximized ones. DockManager.FloatPane and DockManager.DockBackPane do the same on a live manager. A floating window draws its own caption. Drag the caption to move the window, or drop it on a guide to dock the whole window. Double-clicking the caption docks the selected pane back if its previous group is still in the main tree, and maximizes the window otherwise. On a maximized float, a click or a press without movement leaves it maximized. A double-click restores its earlier place and size. Dragging the caption restores that size under the pointer, and the drag continues with the guides. Auto-hide DockEdit.AutoHide moves a tool onto an auto-hide strip on one edge of the dock root. The pane must have CanAutoHide set. DockEdit.Pin docks it back. A new auto-hide entry gets a flyout size of 240 device-independent pixels. public static void Move(DockLayout layout) { DockEdit.Dock(layout, "readme", "docs", DockSide.Right); DockEdit.Float(layout, "readme", 80, 60, 480, 320); DockEdit.DockBack(layout, "readme"); DockEdit.AutoHide(layout, "solution", AutoHideEdge.Left); DockEdit.Pin(layout, "solution"); DockEdit.Select(layout, "program"); } DockManager.AutoHidePane and DockManager.PinPane do the same on a live manager. The flyout is a native child window of the dock, so it paints above HwndHost content in other panes. Because it is a separate window, it opens at full size instead of sliding in. Drag and drop guides Drag a tab along its strip to reorder it. Drag it off the strip to float the pane, then release over a guide to dock it. While you drag, the dock shows a compass over the tab group under the pointer and one button at the middle of each edge of the host. A compass side button splits that leaf in half. The preview shows the same slice the drop inserts. The compass center button adds the pane as a tab of that group. An edge button docks against the root and takes one quarter of the host. A root-edge button wins when it overlaps the compass. A tool, or a float made of tools, can also drop on an auto-hide strip. A document has no auto-hide target. When the pointer is over another floating window, that window's compass and edge buttons are shown. The topmost window wins, and the window being dragged is skipped. Guides and the drop preview are drawn in a topmost overlay, so the window you drag never covers them. Dropping a single torn-off pane calls DockEdit.Dock. Dropping a whole window calls DockEdit.DockWindow: a side button keeps the window's tree as it is, and the center button appends its panes to the target group. Hide and show DockEdit.Hide takes a pane out of the tree and stores it on DockLayout.Hidden, along with the place DockEdit.Show puts it back. Hiding works even when CanClose is false. A hidden pane isn't drawn and doesn't appear in the Ctrl+Tab switcher. On a live manager, use DockManager.HidePane and DockManager.ShowPane. Events and callbacks lists the events a hide raises.

articles/mvvm.html.title: MVVM | SmartDock
articles/mvvm.html.summary: MVVM Bind DocumentsSource, ToolsSource, ActiveContent, and SavedLayout, and the view model can drive the whole dock without touching the control. In ShellWindow the code-behind only calls InitializeComponent. ShellViewModel holds the documents, two tools, one toolbar, and the saved layout string, and never references DockManager. You don't need an MVVM framework: the sample uses a small RelayCommand, and the view models implement INotifyPropertyChanged. <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.ShellWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" xmlns:local="clr-namespace:SmartDock.Docs.Samples" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <Window.DataContext> <local:ShellViewModel /> </Window.DataContext> <Window.Resources> <Style x:Key="DocumentItem" TargetType="dock:DockItem"> <Setter Property="Title" Value="{Binding Title}" /> <Setter Property="ContentId" Value="{Binding ContentId}" /> <Setter Property="CanClose" Value="{Binding CanClose}" /> <Setter Property="CanFloat" Value="{Binding CanFloat}" /> </Style> <Style x:Key="ToolItem" TargetType="dock:DockItem"> <Setter Property="Title" Value="{Binding Title}" /> <Setter Property="ContentId" Value="{Binding ContentId}" /> <Setter Property="CanClose" Value="{Binding CanClose}" /> <Setter Property="CanFloat" Value="{Binding CanFloat}" /> <Setter Property="CanAutoHide" Value="{Binding CanAutoHide}" /> <Setter Property="HideOnClose" Value="{Binding HideOnClose}" /> </Style> <Style x:Key="BarItem" TargetType="dock:DockToolBarItem"> <Setter Property="Id" Value="{Binding Id}" /> <Setter Property="Title" Value="{Binding Title}" /> <Setter Property="Edge" Value="{Binding Edge}" /> </Style> <DataTemplate x:Key="TextBody"> <TextBox Text="{Binding Text, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" AcceptsReturn="True" BorderThickness="0" /> </DataTemplate> <DataTemplate x:Key="NoteBody"> <TextBox Text="{Binding Text, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" AcceptsReturn="True" BorderThickness="0" FontStyle="Italic" /> </DataTemplate> <local:ShellTemplateSelector x:Key="Documents" Text="{StaticResource TextBody}" Note="{StaticResource NoteBody}" /> <DataTemplate x:Key="ToolBody"> <TextBlock Text="{Binding Text}" Margin="12" TextWrapping="Wrap" /> </DataTemplate> <DataTemplate x:Key="ShellBar"> <ToolBar> <Button Content="New" Command="{Binding NewDocument}" /> </ToolBar> </DataTemplate> </Window.Resources> <DockPanel> <StackPanel DockPanel.Dock="Top" Orientation="Horizontal" Margin="4"> <Button Content="Save layout" Margin="0,0,4,0" Command="{x:Static dock:DockCommands.SaveLayout}" CommandTarget="{Binding ElementName=Dock}" /> <Button Content="Restore layout" Command="{x:Static dock:DockCommands.LoadLayout}" CommandTarget="{Binding ElementName=Dock}" /> </StackPanel> <TextBlock DockPanel.Dock="Bottom" Margin="8,4" Text="{Binding ActiveTitle}" /> <dock:DockManager x:Name="Dock" DocumentItemStyle="{StaticResource DocumentItem}" ToolItemStyle="{StaticResource ToolItem}" DocumentTemplateSelector="{StaticResource Documents}" ToolTemplate="{StaticResource ToolBody}" ToolBarItemStyle="{StaticResource BarItem}" ToolBarTemplate="{StaticResource ShellBar}" DocumentsSource="{Binding Documents}" ToolsSource="{Binding Tools}" ToolBarsSource="{Binding ToolBars}" ActiveContent="{Binding Active, Mode=TwoWay}" SavedLayout="{Binding Layout}" /> </DockPanel> </Window> Pane items DocumentItemStyle and ToolItemStyle target DockItem, with the source item as the data context, so the setters bind straight to the view model: using System.ComponentModel; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public abstract class DocumentViewModel : INotifyPropertyChanged { private string _title; protected DocumentViewModel(string contentId, string title) { ContentId = contentId; _title = title; } public string ContentId { get; } public string Title { get => _title; set { _title = value; OnPropertyChanged(); } } public bool CanClose { get; protected set; } = true; public bool CanFloat { get; protected set; } = true; public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged; protected void OnPropertyChanged([CallerMemberName] string? name = null) => PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); } using System.ComponentModel; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public sealed class ToolViewModel : INotifyPropertyChanged { private string _title; private string _text; public ToolViewModel(string contentId, string title, string text, bool canClose, bool canAutoHide, bool hideOnClose) { ContentId = contentId; _title = title; _text = text; CanClose = canClose; CanAutoHide = canAutoHide; HideOnClose = hideOnClose; } public string ContentId { get; } public string Title { get => _title; set { _title = value; OnPropertyChanged(); } } public string Text { get => _text; set { _text = value; OnPropertyChanged(); } } public bool CanClose { get; } public bool CanFloat => true; public bool CanAutoHide { get; } public bool HideOnClose { get; } public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged; private void OnPropertyChanged([CallerMemberName] string? name = null) => PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); } DockItem has Title, ContentId, Icon, CanClose, CanFloat, CanAutoHide, and HideOnClose. A pane with an empty title shows its content id. An empty ContentId is replaced with item- followed by eight hex digits. A saved layout matches items by id, so these view models use fixed ids. Icon isn't saved in the layout file. CanAutoHide defaults to true for tools whose style doesn't set it. This style binds it, so the view model decides. The close button appears when CanClose or HideOnClose is true. Solution Explorer sets CanClose to false and has no close button. Output sets HideOnClose, so closing it hides the pane and leaves the item in Tools. When the user closes a pane, the manager removes the item from the source if the source is a writable IList, which ObservableCollection is. If the source isn't a list, the item stays, and the manager remembers that the user closed it, so resetting the same collection won't reopen it until the item is really removed. For documents, DocumentTemplateSelector runs first. If it returns null, DocumentTemplate is used, and then the implicit DataTemplate for the item's type. ShellTemplateSelector returns the text template, the note template, or null: using System.Windows; using System.Windows.Controls; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public sealed class ShellTemplateSelector : DataTemplateSelector { public DataTemplate? Text { get; set; } public DataTemplate? Note { get; set; } public override DataTemplate? SelectTemplate(object item, DependencyObject container) { if (item is TextDocumentViewModel) return Text; if (item is NoteDocumentViewModel) return Note; return null; } } Tools follow the same order with ToolTemplateSelector and ToolTemplate. This window sets ToolTemplate and no selector. Templates are ignored for items that are themselves a UIElement. Implicit templates in Window.Resources work too, since the manager looks them up again when it gets a parent and when it loads; Working in XAML uses that approach. The manager reads the item style when an item is added and again whenever a bound property changes. Title raises PropertyChanged on the view model, so the tab text follows it. Active pane ActiveContent binds two-way by default. The manager writes it with SetCurrentValue, so your binding stays in place. Setting Active on the view model shows and activates that pane, even if it was hidden or auto-hidden. The value is null when the active pane didn't come from DocumentsSource or ToolsSource. ActiveTitle reads the same object, so the status line follows the selection. If you set the active item before it's in a source, the manager keeps the value and activates the item once it appears. Where new panes go The sample never sets DockManager.Layout; the sources build the tree. The first pane of an empty manager becomes the root. A new document joins the main-tree document group that last held the active document. If there isn't one, it joins the first document group, and if there are no document groups, it goes to the right of the root at 0.75. A new tool joins the first tool group, or goes to the left of the root at 0.25. An item whose content id is already in the layout stays where the layout put it, whether that's a floating window, an auto-hide strip, or the hidden list. NewDocument adds a TextDocumentViewModel with a new content id and sets Active, which activates the new pane: private void AddDocument() { _next++; var document = new TextDocumentViewModel("doc-" + _next, "Document " + _next, ""); Documents.Add(document); Active = document; } Toolbars ToolBarsSource builds one ToolBar per item, using ToolBarTemplateSelector, then ToolBarTemplate, then the implicit DataTemplate. The template's root must be a ToolBar; if it isn't, the manager ignores the template and creates an empty toolbar. The toolbar's data context is set to the item unless the toolbar already has one. Placement comes from DockToolBarItem, not from the DockToolBar attached properties. ToolBarItemStyle targets DockToolBarItem and here binds Id, Title, and Edge. You can also set Band, BandIndex, Offset, Alignment, PaneId, IsVisible, ShowOverflow, and IsCustomizable. They're read when the toolbar is added and whenever a binding changes, but Edge and the band properties only place a toolbar that doesn't have a position yet. Toolbars explains each value. using System.Windows.Input; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public sealed class ToolBarViewModel { private readonly ShellViewModel _shell; public ToolBarViewModel(ShellViewModel shell) => _shell = shell; public string Id => "standard"; public string Title => "Standard"; public ToolBarEdge Edge => ToolBarEdge.Top; public ICommand NewDocument => _shell.NewDocument; } The New button binds to NewDocument on the toolbar view model, which forwards the shell's command, so it keeps working when the toolbar is torn off into its own window. ElementName bindings don't resolve inside the template. Save and load SavedLayout binds two-way by default, here to the view model's Layout string. The Save button runs DockCommands.SaveLayout with CommandTarget set to the manager, since the button is outside it; a button or menu item inside the manager doesn't need CommandTarget. The manager and each floating window handle the command. It writes the current layout to SavedLayout with SetCurrentValue, so the binding pushes the JSON into the view model's Layout property and the dock doesn't reload. If no layout has been assigned yet, the command does nothing, but by the time the window is shown the sources have already built one. public string? Layout { get => _layout; set { if (_layout == value) return; _layout = value; OnPropertyChanged(); } } Any other change to SavedLayout loads the text exactly like LoadLayout. That includes a value set before the window is shown, so the first frame already uses it. Null and the empty string are ignored, but a string of spaces isn't empty. Text that LoadLayout can't read throws DockLayoutException and leaves the current tree alone. The SaveLayout method throws InvalidOperationException when no layout is assigned, which is why the command checks first. The Restore button runs DockCommands.LoadLayout, with CommandTarget set to the manager. The command loads the current SavedLayout, so it puts the last save back even when that string has not changed. CanExecute is false when SavedLayout is null or empty, and the command does nothing in that case. Bad JSON throws DockLayoutException and leaves the tree as it is. A non-empty CommandParameter is loaded in place of SavedLayout, and that text is written back to SavedLayout without loading a second time. The string is the same JSON described in Saving and loading layouts. It stores content ids, not view models. Loading replaces DockManager.Layout. A pane whose content id is still in Documents or Tools keeps its item, and a source item missing from the file opens at the default place described above. An id in the file that's no longer in a source and has no factory shows a "Missing content: id" placeholder. Because closing a document removes it from Documents, a layout saved before the close still names it. RelayCommand is the entire command implementation, used by NewDocument. using System.Windows.Input; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public sealed class RelayCommand : ICommand { private readonly Action<object?> _execute; private readonly Predicate<object?>? _canExecute; public RelayCommand(Action<object?> execute, Predicate<object?>? canExecute = null) { _execute = execute; _canExecute = canExecute; } public bool CanExecute(object? parameter) => _canExecute?.Invoke(parameter) ?? true; public void Execute(object? parameter) => _execute(parameter); public event EventHandler? CanExecuteChanged { add => CommandManager.RequerySuggested += value; remove => CommandManager.RequerySuggested -= value; } } Next: Saving and loading layouts.

articles/saving-layouts.html.title: Saving and loading layouts | SmartDock
articles/saving-layouts.html.summary: Saving and loading layouts DockSerializer turns a layout into one line of compact JSON and back. The format version is DockLayout.CurrentVersion, currently 1. Serialize validates the tree before writing. Deserialize throws DockLayoutException when the JSON is malformed or the tree fails validation. That covers a version other than 1, a missing or repeated id, a split with fewer than two children, an empty tab group that no hidden entry points to, and a non-finite number where a finite one is required. A round trip is exact: a document written by Serialize reads back as an equal layout and writes out as the same bytes. The file keeps ids, weights, the selected tab, float bounds and the maximized flag, auto-hide entries, hidden panes, and toolbar state. When DockLayout.ToolBars is null, the file has no toolBars object at all. Enums are written as lowercase strings, and each node has "type": "split" or "type": "tabs". public static string CoreRoundTrip(DockLayout layout) { string json = DockSerializer.Serialize(layout); DockLayout restored = DockSerializer.Deserialize(json); return DockSerializer.Serialize(restored); } With a DockManager, use SaveLayout and LoadLayout. SaveLayout copies the current toolbar positions into the layout before it serializes, and throws InvalidOperationException when no layout is assigned. LoadLayout deserializes and assigns Layout. Call it before the window is shown, or while the manager is hidden, so the first frame on screen is the saved layout. Loading raises PaneStateChanged for panes whose state changed. It never raises PaneClosing or PaneClosed. SavedLayout is a string dependency property, null by default, and it binds both ways. DockCommands.SaveLayout serializes the current layout and writes that property with SetCurrentValue, so a binding updates the source and the tree is not loaded again. Any other change, including a binding update, loads the text the same way LoadLayout does. A value set before the manager is loaded is applied then, so the first frame is that layout. Null or an empty string does nothing. Text LoadLayout cannot read throws DockLayoutException and leaves the current tree in place. A string of spaces is not empty. The save command does nothing when no layout is assigned. Assigning the same string again does not load, because the property has not changed. DockCommands.LoadLayout loads the current SavedLayout anyway. It does nothing when that string is null or empty, and bad JSON throws DockLayoutException and leaves the tree in place. A non-empty command parameter is loaded instead, then written with SetCurrentValue, so that write does not load a second time. The manager and each floating window handle the command, and it has no default key. public static void ManagerRoundTrip(DockManager dock, string path) { File.WriteAllText(path, dock.SaveLayout()); dock.LoadLayout(File.ReadAllText(path)); } DockSerializer.SerializeUtf8 writes the same document as UTF-8 bytes. DockLayout.Clone makes a deep copy through the same JSON and also copies DockPane.PreviousGroupId, which the file doesn't store. The theme, the Ctrl+Tab activation order, and pane icons are not saved. Restore them yourself if you need them.

articles/styling.html.title: Styling and templates | SmartDock
articles/styling.html.summary: Styling and templates To restyle the chrome, put an implicit style in DockManager.Resources. Floating windows, the guide overlay, the auto-hide flyout, and toolbar windows are separate visual trees and can't see the manager's resources, so the manager copies styles for these types onto each of them: DockTabHeader, DockCaption, DockDropPreview, DockGuideButton, DockToolBarGrip, DockToolBarTray, DockToolBarCaption, DockToolBarDrop, and DockToolBarCustomize. A style in Application.Resources doesn't need copying, because every window already sees it. Each of those controls picks up the implicit style from its manager when it loads, and assigning Theme makes chrome that is already open pick it up again. If you remove a style from the manager, the control drops it and goes back to the template in Themes/Generic.xaml. Theme brushes The chrome reads these keys: Dock.Workspace, Dock.Panel, Dock.Chrome, Dock.Header, Dock.Border, Dock.Text, Dock.Muted, Dock.Accent, Dock.AccentSoft, Dock.AccentInactive, Dock.Guide, Dock.GuideButton, Dock.GuideBorder, Dock.Hover, and Dock.Font. DockTheme has a *Key constant for each one, such as DockTheme.AccentKey. Dock.FocusVisual is the focus rectangle, drawn with Dock.Accent. Dock.GuideBorder is transparent in every built-in theme. Dock.Accent is the bright edge of the active pane. Dock.AccentInactive is the same edge when that tab is selected, or that lone caption is showing, but the pane is not the active one. A Dock.AccentInactive brush in DockManager.Resources wins the same way the other Dock.* keys do. The theme palette lives in a dictionary that the manager merges into its resources. A Dock.* key you add to DockManager.Resources sits above that dictionary, so it wins over the theme and keeps winning after the manager loads and after Theme changes. Your overrides are also copied onto floating windows, the guide overlay, the auto-hide flyout, toolbar windows, the toolbar name dialog, the Edit Custom Toolbars dialog, and the Delete Toolbar confirmation window. If you add an override after one of those windows is open, it reaches that window the next time Theme is assigned (assigning the current value is enough) and every new window gets it when it is created. DockManager.CustomTheme is a shared dictionary of the same keys. It sits under those local keys and over the palette. The New Toolbar, Rename, Edit Custom Toolbars, and Delete Toolbar dialogs use these brushes for the window, caption, text box, list, and buttons. Themes has the class, the order, and which key paints which part. StylingWindow binds Theme and replaces the accent brushes, including the dim edge: <Window.DataContext> <local:ThemeChoice /> </Window.DataContext> <dock:DockManager x:Name="Dock" local:SampleContent.Prepare="True" Theme="{Binding Theme}"> <dock:DockManager.Resources> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="{x:Static dock:DockTheme.AccentKey}" Color="#FFC45C26" /> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="{x:Static dock:DockTheme.AccentSoftKey}" Color="#FFF0D3C2" /> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="{x:Static dock:DockTheme.AccentInactiveKey}" Color="#FF8C5A3C" /> The Blue button switches the bound property to DockThemeKind.Blue, and the copper accent stays. Don't point x:Static at DockTheme.Border or DockTheme.Panel, because those names clash with WPF types; use the *Key constants. Themes covers DockTheme.Apply, the menu dictionary, and the scroll bar dictionary. The panes in this sample get their controls from SampleContent.Prepare, because RegisterContent can't be called from markup. Working in XAML explains why. Tab headers <Style TargetType="dock:DockTabHeader"> <Setter Property="Focusable" Value="False" /> <Setter Property="Margin" Value="2,4,2,0" /> <Setter Property="Padding" Value="8,4" /> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Header}" /> <Setter Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Border}" /> <Setter Property="BorderThickness" Value="0,0,0,2" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockTabHeader"> <Border x:Name="PART_Chrome" Background="{TemplateBinding Background}" BorderBrush="{TemplateBinding BorderBrush}" BorderThickness="{TemplateBinding BorderThickness}" Padding="{TemplateBinding Padding}"> <StackPanel x:Name="PART_ButtonHost" Orientation="Horizontal"> <TextBlock Text="{TemplateBinding Title}" VerticalAlignment="Center" Margin="4,0" Foreground="{DynamicResource Dock.Text}" FontFamily="{DynamicResource Dock.Font}" /> </StackPanel> </Border> <ControlTemplate.Triggers> <Trigger Property="IsSelected" Value="True"> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Panel}" /> <Setter Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.AccentInactive}" /> </Trigger> <MultiTrigger> <MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Condition Property="IsSelected" Value="True" /> <Condition Property="IsActive" Value="True" /> </MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Setter Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Accent}" /> </MultiTrigger> <Trigger Property="Placement" Value="Bottom"> <Setter Property="Margin" Value="2,0,2,4" /> </Trigger> </ControlTemplate.Triggers> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> PART_ButtonHost is where the header puts its buttons when the template doesn't provide its own. It gets a close button if the pane can close or has HideOnClose, and a pin if the pane can auto-hide. They're added after the template's own children, in the order pin, close, menu. To supply your own button, name a Button PART_Close, PART_Pin, or PART_Menu; the header collapses it whenever that action isn't available. ShowMenu stays false, so a PART_Menu button stays collapsed. PART_Face is optional. If the template names both PART_Face and PART_ButtonHost, the header lays the face over the accent stroke and the padding; otherwise the template keeps its own layout. PART_Chrome is the outer border. The default style fills it with theme brushes, and a replaced style is left to paint itself. The header exposes Title, Icon, IsSelected, IsActive, Kind, Placement, IsHovered, ShowClose, ShowPin, and ShowMenu for your template to bind. Dragging, selecting, and closing are handled by the control, so they keep working with any template. IsActive is true when this header's group holds the active pane. The default selected tab keeps the panel fill and draws a 2px Dock.Accent edge while IsActive is true, and Dock.AccentInactive while it is false. An unselected tab keeps the header fill and no edge. A replaced style is left alone: the sample paints Dock.AccentInactive when IsSelected is true, and Dock.Accent when IsSelected and IsActive are both true. Switching the active pane repaints the headers. There is one bright edge, on the active pane. Captions <Style TargetType="dock:DockCaption"> <Setter Property="Focusable" Value="False" /> <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="32" /> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Chrome}" /> <Setter Property="Foreground" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Text}" /> <Setter Property="FontFamily" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Font}" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockCaption"> <Border x:Name="PART_Chrome" Background="{TemplateBinding Background}" MinHeight="{TemplateBinding MinHeight}"> <DockPanel x:Name="PART_Bar" LastChildFill="True"> <StackPanel x:Name="PART_Buttons" DockPanel.Dock="Right" Orientation="Horizontal" VerticalAlignment="Center" /> <Border x:Name="PART_Grip" Background="{TemplateBinding Background}"> <Grid> <ContentPresenter /> <StackPanel x:Name="TitleRow" Orientation="Horizontal" IsHitTestVisible="False"> <TextBlock x:Name="PART_Title" Text="{TemplateBinding Title}" Margin="10,0,8,0" VerticalAlignment="Center" Foreground="{TemplateBinding Foreground}" FontFamily="{TemplateBinding FontFamily}" /> </StackPanel> </Grid> </Border> </DockPanel> </Border> <ControlTemplate.Triggers> <Trigger Property="Role" Value="Strip"> <Setter TargetName="TitleRow" Property="Visibility" Value="Collapsed" /> </Trigger> <Trigger Property="IsAccented" Value="True"> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Panel}" /> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.AccentInactive}" /> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderThickness" Value="0,2,0,0" /> </Trigger> <MultiTrigger> <MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Condition Property="IsAccented" Value="True" /> <Condition Property="IsActive" Value="True" /> </MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Accent}" /> </MultiTrigger> <Trigger Property="Role" Value="Flyout"> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.AccentInactive}" /> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderThickness" Value="0,2,0,0" /> </Trigger> <MultiTrigger> <MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Condition Property="Role" Value="Flyout" /> <Condition Property="IsActive" Value="True" /> </MultiTrigger.Conditions> <Setter TargetName="PART_Chrome" Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Accent}" /> </MultiTrigger> </ControlTemplate.Triggers> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> A custom caption style hosts the library's button cluster in PART_Buttons. If you name a Button PART_Close, PART_Pin, PART_Maximize, or PART_Menu, the caption gives it the library button's automation name, tooltip, glyph, and visibility, and takes the library button out of the cluster so it doesn't show twice. A template with neither the named button nor PART_Buttons simply has no such button. The default template, used while Style is null, puts the cluster in PART_Bar instead. PART_Grip is the drag surface; without it, the whole caption is. A strip caption (Role is Strip) shows the tab strip as its content, so its template needs a ContentPresenter. The sample hides the title row for that role. PART_Title shows Title, and a template without it shows no title. IsAccented is true for the one-pane top bar. That bar uses the panel fill and a 2px edge. The edge is Dock.Accent while IsActive is true and Dock.AccentInactive while it is false. IsActive is true when this caption's pane is the active pane. A split float title is active while that window is active, and it does not draw this edge. A replaced style reads IsAccented and IsActive and paints itself. The sample uses Dock.AccentInactive for the accented bar and Dock.Accent when that bar is also active. A flyout caption stays IsAccented false and keeps the chrome fill, at 28px unless your style sets a height. Its 2px top edge still follows IsActive. The sample paints that edge from Role being Flyout. A bottom tool caption, with tabs under the content and more than one pane, keeps the chrome fill and draws no edge. Drop preview and guides <Style TargetType="dock:DockDropPreview"> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Guide}" /> <Setter Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Accent}" /> <Setter Property="BorderThickness" Value="1" /> <Setter Property="CornerRadius" Value="2" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockDropPreview"> <Border Background="{TemplateBinding Background}" BorderBrush="{TemplateBinding BorderBrush}" BorderThickness="{TemplateBinding BorderThickness}" CornerRadius="{TemplateBinding CornerRadius}" /> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> DockDropPreview has no named parts. SmartDock.Core decides where the rectangle goes, and the template only paints it. CornerRadius is a property on the control. The default border thickness is 0 and Dock.GuideBorder is transparent, so the stock preview is a plain fill; the sample adds a 1px accent edge. The preview never takes mouse input. DockGuideButton names PART_Chrome, PART_Plate, and PART_Mark. Hit testing uses the guide rectangles in SmartDock.Core, so the button doesn't take mouse input either. The library moves PART_Mark only while Style is null; a replaced style draws its own icon. Side is Left, Right, Top, Bottom, or Center, where Center tabs the pane into the group. IsRootEdge is true for the buttons in the middle of a host edge, and IsHot is true while the pointer is over the guide. The default template switches to the accent fill when IsHot is true. Toolbar chrome <Style TargetType="dock:DockToolBarTray"> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Chrome}" /> <Setter Property="BorderBrush" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Border}" /> <Setter Property="BorderThickness" Value="0,0,0,1" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockToolBarTray"> <Border Background="{TemplateBinding Background}" BorderBrush="{TemplateBinding BorderBrush}" BorderThickness="{TemplateBinding BorderThickness}"> <StackPanel x:Name="PART_Bands" /> </Border> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> <Style TargetType="dock:DockToolBarGrip"> <Setter Property="MinWidth" Value="14" /> <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="14" /> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Header}" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockToolBarGrip"> <Border Background="{TemplateBinding Background}" /> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> <Style TargetType="dock:DockToolBarCaption"> <Setter Property="Background" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Chrome}" /> <Setter Property="MinHeight" Value="22" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockToolBarCaption"> <Border Background="{TemplateBinding Background}"> <DockPanel LastChildFill="True"> <Button x:Name="PART_Close" DockPanel.Dock="Right" Width="22" Focusable="False" Content="×" Foreground="{DynamicResource Dock.Text}" /> <dock:DockToolBarGrip x:Name="PART_Grip" DockPanel.Dock="Left" /> <TextBlock x:Name="PART_Title" Text="{TemplateBinding Title}" Margin="6,0" VerticalAlignment="Center" Foreground="{DynamicResource Dock.Text}" FontFamily="{DynamicResource Dock.Font}" /> </DockPanel> </Border> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> <Style TargetType="dock:DockToolBarCustomize"> <Setter Property="Foreground" Value="{DynamicResource Dock.Accent}" /> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockToolBarCustomize"> <Border Background="Transparent"> <Path Data="M 1,1 L 5,5 L 9,1" Stroke="{TemplateBinding Foreground}" StrokeThickness="1.2" HorizontalAlignment="Center" VerticalAlignment="Center" Width="10" Height="6" /> </Border> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> DockToolBarTray adds one child per band to PART_Bands, which must be a Panel. If it's a StackPanel, the tray sets it to Horizontal on the left and right edges and Vertical on the top and bottom. Without PART_Bands the tray has nowhere to put bands, so it is removed and its toolbars don't appear. DockToolBarGrip has no named parts. Its Orientation is Horizontal in a top or bottom band and Vertical in a left or right band, where the grip sits at the top. DockToolBarCaption is the title bar of a floating toolbar. PART_Close hides every visible toolbar in that window. On a vertical float that button is a 32/3 DIP box (about 10.7) and its glyph is two thirds of the template's font size. A close button from the host's own template gets the same size. A horizontal caption keeps the width and font size from the template. PART_Grip drags the whole window, and double-clicking PART_Grip docks them all back. PART_Title shows Title. A shared window joins the toolbar titles with a comma. The text trims when the window is narrow, and a trimmed title has a tooltip with the full text. The caption's context menu has Vertical, Dock Back, and Close. Vertical flips every toolbar in the window, and Dock Back and Close act on all of them. Pressing anywhere on the caption except a button also starts a drag, even without PART_Grip, and double-clicking the caption docks the window back too. Without PART_Close there is no close button. A grip on one toolbar still drags, reorders, or tears off that toolbar, and double-clicking it docks only that one. DockToolBarCustomize is the chevron that opens the Add or Remove Buttons menu. It has no named parts, and Click is handled by the control, so a replaced template still opens the menu. DockToolBarDrop is the line shown while you drag a toolbar. It has no named parts, doesn't take mouse input, and is filled with Dock.Accent by default. Leaving parts out <ResourceDictionary xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock"> <!-- Not merged by StylingWindow. A header template with neither PART_Close nor PART_ButtonHost has no close button. --> <Style TargetType="dock:DockTabHeader"> <Setter Property="Template"> <Setter.Value> <ControlTemplate TargetType="dock:DockTabHeader"> <TextBlock Text="{TemplateBinding Title}" Margin="8,4" VerticalAlignment="Center" Foreground="{DynamicResource Dock.Text}" FontFamily="{DynamicResource Dock.Font}" /> </ControlTemplate> </Setter.Value> </Setter> </Style> </ResourceDictionary> StylingWindow doesn't use this dictionary. It's here to show what happens when a part is missing. Used as the implicit DockTabHeader style, it gives headers with no close button and no pin, because the template names neither the buttons nor PART_ButtonHost. Dragging and selecting still work. A caption works the same way: if it names neither PART_Buttons nor PART_Close, it has no close button. Next: Working in XAML.

articles/themes.html.title: Themes | SmartDock
articles/themes.html.summary: Themes DockManager.Theme is a dependency property. Set it to DockThemeKind.Dark (the default), Light, or Blue, or bind it. The palette lives in a dictionary the manager merges. A Dock.* entry in DockManager.Resources is left in place and wins, including after the manager loads and after Theme changes. The same entry is copied onto floating windows, the guide overlay, the auto-hide flyout, toolbar windows, the toolbar name dialog, the Edit Custom Toolbars dialog, and the Delete Toolbar confirmation window. An override added after one of those windows exists is copied the next time Theme is assigned, including to the value it already has, and when that window is created. The pane switcher follows the theme. Open chrome repaints in place. The theme is not saved with the layout. public static void UseLight(DockManager dock) { dock.Theme = DockThemeKind.Light; } To use the dock palette outside the manager, for example in a dictionary merged into Application.Resources, call DockTheme.Apply on any FrameworkElement or ResourceDictionary. public static void ApplyBlue(FrameworkElement element) { DockTheme.Apply(element, DockThemeKind.Blue); } The chrome looks brushes up by resource key, not through the static brush properties. The keys are Dock.Workspace, Dock.Panel, Dock.Chrome, Dock.Header, Dock.Border, Dock.Text, Dock.Muted, Dock.Accent, Dock.AccentSoft, Dock.AccentInactive, Dock.Guide, Dock.GuideButton, Dock.GuideBorder, Dock.Hover, and Dock.Font. DockTheme exposes each name as a *Key constant, for example DockTheme.WorkspaceKey. Dock.AccentInactive is the edge of a selected tab or lone caption whose pane is not active. Dark, light, and blue each define it. A DockCustomTheme dictionary may set Dock.AccentInactive, and a local override wins like the other Dock.* keys. New Toolbar, Rename, Edit Custom Toolbars, and Delete Toolbar use a separate window, and it reads the same keys. The window background is Dock.Panel and the edge is Dock.Border. The caption is Dock.Chrome with Dock.Text. The text box uses Dock.Chrome, Dock.Text for the text and the caret, and Dock.Border, and that border becomes Dock.Accent while the box has focus. The toolbar list uses Dock.Panel, Dock.Text, and Dock.Border. The selected row uses Dock.AccentSoft. OK, Cancel, Rename, Delete, and Close use Dock.Chrome, Dock.Text, and Dock.Border. Hover uses Dock.Hover, a press uses Dock.AccentSoft, and keyboard focus uses Dock.Accent plus Dock.FocusVisual. A custom theme and a Dock.* entry on the manager reach these dialogs, including while one is open. An empty or duplicate name still leaves the dialog up, with no extra message. Delete asks in the Edit Custom Toolbars dialog. Delete Toolbar on Add or Remove Buttons asks in its own window with the same caption, text, and buttons. The static brushes on DockTheme always hold the dark palette, and the chrome doesn't use them. Don't reference DockTheme.Border or DockTheme.Panel with x:Static: those names match WPF types, and the markup compiler resolves them as types. DockTheme.CreateScrollBarResources returns styles for the scroll bar, tool tip, and focus visual. The manager, each floating window, the switcher, the toolbar name dialog, the Edit Custom Toolbars dialog, and the Delete Toolbar confirmation window merge it already. Merge your own copy if you want the same scroll bars elsewhere in the app. DockTheme.CreateMenuResources returns menu, context menu, menu item, and separator styles in the dock colors. Nothing merges it for you. Merge it into application resources if your menus should match the dock, or leave it out to keep the system look. A copy merged into the host window follows Theme changes. A shared dictionary DockManager.CustomTheme points a manager at a resource dictionary you already share across windows. Subclass DockCustomTheme and return that dictionary's Uri. You do not write the Uri on each window. public sealed class EditorDockTheme : DockCustomTheme { public override Uri GetResourceUri() => new("/MyApp;component/Themes/EditorDock.xaml", UriKind.Relative); } The dictionary can hold other styles. SmartDock reads Dock.* and DockMenu.* only, including keys that come from a dictionary merged into it. A key it does not define stays on Theme. <ResourceDictionary xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="Dock.Chrome" Color="#FF2A241C" /> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="Dock.Panel" Color="#FF3A3228" /> <SolidColorBrush x:Key="DockMenu.Panel" Color="#FF3A3228" /> </ResourceDictionary> <sd:DockManager Theme="Dark"> <sd:DockManager.CustomTheme> <local:EditorDockTheme /> </sd:DockManager.CustomTheme> </sd:DockManager> When several brushes define the same key, the winner is: A Dock.* or DockMenu.* key set on DockManager.Resources itself. The same key in the custom dictionary. DockManager.Theme. Setting, replacing, or clearing CustomTheme repaints chrome that is already open, including the toolbar name dialog, the Edit Custom Toolbars dialog, and the Delete Toolbar confirmation window, and windows opened later pick it up. Changing Theme leaves the custom keys in place. Set CustomTheme to null to go back to the palette. A Uri that cannot be loaded throws when you set the property, and the previous theme stays. The choice is not saved with the layout.

articles/toolbars.html.title: Toolbars | SmartDock
articles/toolbars.html.summary: Toolbars Put ordinary WPF ToolBar controls in DockManager.ToolBars and the dock lays them out in trays on the main window or on a pane, including a pane inside a floating window. A floating pane window has no trays of its own: the caption and the outside edges are not drop targets. An open auto-hide flyout is a pane, so a toolbar can dock to it. If you never touch ToolBars or ToolBarsSource, no tray is built. Set DockToolBar attached properties on each toolbar to say where it goes: Property Meaning Id Stable id. A saved entry is matched to the toolbar by this string. The toolbar's Name is used when Id is empty. Title Caption of a floating toolbar, and the label in the tray menu. Edge Top, Bottom, Left, or Right. The default is Top. Band Row or column on that edge. Band 0 is the outer side: the top of a top tray, the bottom of a bottom tray, the left of a left tray, and the right of a right tray. BandIndex Position within the band. Offset Gap before the toolbar, in device-independent pixels. Alignment Start packs from the left of a horizontal band or the top of a vertical one. End packs from the right or the bottom. Start is the default. Dragging a toolbar so its trailing edge reaches the far end, or comes within 16 device-independent pixels of it, pins it to End. Dragging it back off that zone packs it from the start. PaneId Content id of the pane that hosts the toolbar. Empty means a window tray. A pane that is not in the layout uses the main window's top tray. IsVisible False hides the toolbar and keeps a floating window's bounds. True shows it again. ShowOverflow When true, the toolbar uses the leftover space in the band and shows an overflow chevron. The default is false. IsCustomizable When false, that toolbar has no customize menu and ignores Alt+drag. The default is true. Edge, Band, BandIndex, Offset, Alignment, and PaneId only set the starting place. Once the toolbar has been shown or dragged, its layout entry decides where it is, and changing these properties no longer moves it. Reset on the customize menu is what puts the toolbar back on this place. <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.ToolbarWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <dock:DockManager x:Name="Dock"> <dock:DockManager.ToolBars> <ToolBar dock:DockToolBar.Id="standard" dock:DockToolBar.Title="Standard" dock:DockToolBar.Edge="Top" dock:DockToolBar.Band="0" dock:DockToolBar.Alignment="Start"> <Button Content="Save" /> </ToolBar> </dock:DockManager.ToolBars> </dock:DockManager> </Window> The same thing in code: public static void AddAligned(DockManager dock) { var bar = new ToolBar(); DockToolBar.SetId(bar, "standard"); DockToolBar.SetTitle(bar, "Standard"); DockToolBar.SetEdge(bar, ToolBarEdge.Top); DockToolBar.SetBand(bar, 0); DockToolBar.SetBandIndex(bar, 0); DockToolBar.SetOffset(bar, 0); DockToolBar.SetAlignment(bar, ToolBarAlignment.End); bar.Items.Add(new Button { Name = "save", Content = "Save" }); dock.ToolBars.Add(bar); } To bind toolbars from view models, use ToolBarsSource. Each item becomes a ToolBar built from ToolBarTemplateSelector if set, else ToolBarTemplate, else the implicit data template. Placement comes from DockToolBarItem instead of the attached properties: bind its properties in a style assigned to ToolBarItemStyle. The buttons themselves stay in each toolbar's own Items or ItemsSource. Floating toolbars Drag the grip along the band to slide the toolbar. Drag it out of the tray and it turns into a floating window that follows the pointer; the window is shown on that move, under the pointer, while the button is still down, and release leaves it there. Dragging the caption moves the window with the pointer on each move, the same way a pane float moves. An edge that does not have a band yet shows the drop line in the guide overlay, so a floating toolbar and native pane content do not cover it, and it does not open a tray while the button is down. The pointer over a pane draws the edge guides. The caption and the outside edges of a floating pane window draw no band, and releasing there leaves the toolbar floating. A pane inside that window still takes the drop. The main window's trays are unchanged. Right and bottom lines sit inside the window. A point in an empty edge's zone docks on that edge even when it is also in the slop of a tray on another side. A point inside that tray still uses the tray. The band is created when the toolbar is dropped there. Dropping somewhere else, or pressing Escape, leaves that edge empty. A band that is already there still takes the toolbar while the pointer is down. A new row in a tray that already has bands waits for the drop too, because that row would make the tray taller. The window starts horizontal, including a single line torn off the left or right edge. Moving back over a tray in the same drag docks it again. Double-click the grip of a floating toolbar to send that toolbar back to the band it came from. The close button on the caption hides it, and showing it again reopens the window at the same bounds. A window that holds several toolbars is described below. A floating toolbar can stack its buttons. Right-click the caption and check Vertical. The same item is on Add or Remove Buttons while the toolbar is floating. The grip moves to the top and the Add or Remove Buttons chevron to the bottom. The caption stays on top and does not draw the title; the tooltip is the full text. A horizontal title that does not fit is trimmed, and the tooltip shows the full text. The close button stays usable. The window measures again after the orientation change, including a toolbar the host restyles, so every button stays inside it at any display scale, and the toolbar's overflow chevron appears only when a button does not fit. A vertical float hides the caption grip and makes the caption outside the close button the drag handle, so it is as wide as its button column or the close button (32/3 DIP, about 10.7, with its glyph at two thirds of the template size) when the column is narrower. A column wider than that close button keeps a drag area beside it. Unchecking Vertical measures the window back to the horizontal size. A horizontal float is as wide as its buttons, grip, and chevron, and an empty one is at least as wide as its caption. The button band is the same height as the grip and the chevron, docked or floating: the grip and the chevron start and end where the band does across the row, so a band inset by a template margin, a toolbar margin or height limit, or tray padding still lines up with them. On a vertical row the chevron's width from its style runs down the row and the chevron is as wide as the band. Switching that empty bar to vertical and back measures it again. Combined toolbars in one vertical float share one width, with a separator between them. Drag the right or bottom edge to resize the window. The buttons wrap to fill it: a horizontal window fills each row and then the next, and a vertical window fills each column and then the next. The window snaps to whole cells, so a row of buttons stays one height and there is no empty strip. Each button stays the size the toolbar's own template gave it in one line, including an image with no width or height. The grid keeps the fill, line, corner, padding, and margin of the outermost border the toolbar's template draws around its PART_ToolBarPanel, so a host-styled float looks the same as a grid as it does as one row. A DynamicResource or binding on that border stays live on the grid, so a theme or resource change while the window is a grid updates the fill and the line, and they stay when the float is a single row again. A style that limits the toolbar's height or width is lifted while the grid is shown, so the extra rows and columns stay whole, and those limits come back when the float is a single row or column again. The smallest size is one button plus the caption and the frame. A window at least as wide as it is tall is horizontal, and that includes a square. A taller window is vertical. The Vertical check matches that shape as the edge moves. Press Escape, or lose the mouse capture, and the size and orientation stay as they were when the drag started. SaveLayout writes that width and height with the other float bounds, and loading the layout opens the window at that size. DockManager.SetToolBarFloatVertical and IsToolBarFloatVertical set and read that flag. The setter does nothing while the toolbar is docked. Docking onto a tray, docking back, and Reset clear it. A docked toolbar takes its orientation from the edge: left and right are vertical, top and bottom are horizontal. SaveLayout writes floatVertical only when it is true, so an older file stays the same bytes and loads as horizontal. A file that sets the flag on a toolbar that is not floating loads with it clear. A float of more than one line keeps that count when it docks onto an edge of the same orientation. Horizontal rows stay rows on a top or bottom tray, including a pane tray. Vertical columns stay columns on a left or right edge. Docking onto the other orientation gives one line. ToolBarEntry.Lines is that count.
