Zero means one line and is left out of the file, so a layout saved before line counts existed loads as one line and saves back unchanged. A count of one is also stored as zero. ToolBarBands.SetLines writes it. Every toolbar in one floating window has the same value. ToolBarBands.GridShape is the wrap the float grid uses, and the docked toolbar uses that same grid. The band grows to the grid. The grip and the chevron still start and end where that frame does. A toolbar with ShowOverflow still puts the buttons that do not fit behind the chevron, and the line count stays. Undocking a count above one opens the same grid, so a multi-line toolbar torn off the left or right edge comes back vertical. A single line torn off a side stays horizontal. Reset sets the count back to one line. The count is the number of lines the float shows, so a float with enough buttons hidden to fit one line docks as one line. Merging two floats into one window, or splitting a shared float, resets that window to one line. On a tray too short for the grid, the buttons that do not fit go to the chevron's overflow list, as on a single line, and come back when the tray is long enough. Checking or unchecking Vertical does too, because that sizes the window to one column or one row. Several toolbars can share one floating window. Drag any grip over that window and a 2 device-independent-pixel line shows where it will land. The line is drawn in the guide overlay, so it sits above the float. Drop to insert the toolbar, and the window grows to fit. Drag a grip inside the window to change the order. Drag it out, past the same slop the trays use, and that toolbar becomes its own float under the pointer. The others stay. When one is left, it is an ordinary float again. Dragging the caption moves the whole window. Dropping the caption on a tray or a dock edge docks every visible toolbar in the window, in order. Double-click the caption to send them all back to the bands they left. Double-click one grip to send only that toolbar back. The caption title is the non-custom titles joined with a comma. It trims when it does not fit, and the tooltip is the full list, including a custom toolbar's name. That name is not drawn in the caption. The caption close button and Alt+F4 hide every visible toolbar in the window. They stay floating, in the same group, at the same bounds. Showing one from the tray menu opens the window again at that place. Showing another puts it back in its order. Unchecking one in the tray menu hides only that toolbar. The window shrinks, or hides when nothing in it is visible. Reset on one toolbar docks only that one at its declared place. The orientation belongs to the window. Flipping it flips every toolbar in it. A toolbar dropped into a vertical float becomes vertical. A toolbar torn out of one stays vertical. DockManager.MergeFloatingToolBars(id, targetId, index) puts a toolbar into the window that holds targetId. index is the gap, and a negative index means the end. SplitFloatingToolBar(id) takes one toolbar out at the same place. SaveLayout writes floatId and floatIndex only when they are set, so an older file stays the same bytes. A floatId on a toolbar that is not floating is rejected. A group of one drops floatId when the file is loaded. windowId is not this group. An older file may still have windowId from a toolbar that was docked on a floating pane window's edge. Loading that layout into the dock moves the toolbar to the main window's top tray. A toolbar that was already floating stays floating, and docking it back uses that tray. The next save leaves windowId out. A toolbar with PaneId set travels with its pane when the pane floats, docks somewhere else, changes tabs, or auto-hides. When the pane closes, the toolbar goes back to its declared place. Customize menu and hide or show Users can customize toolbars unless you turn it off. ToolBarCustomizationEnabled is true by default. Right-click an empty part of a tray, the grip, or the chevron to get a menu of all toolbars, listed by title (or id when the title is empty). A floating toolbar opens the same menu from its empty band, its grip, or its chevron. The caption keeps its own menu. A button opens this list only when it has no menu of its own: if the button, or anything between the click and the toolbar, has a context menu, that menu opens and the list does not. If the button opens its own popup from the right-click, the list stays closed, even when that handler does not set Handled. A button with no menu of its own still opens the list. A right-click on an item in the toolbar's overflow keeps the overflow open and follows the same rule. The same applies to a toolbar on a pane in an auto-hide flyout. Visible ones are checked; uncheck one to hide it. Checking or unchecking a toolbar leaves the menu open. New Toolbar and Edit Custom Toolbars close it. Edit Custom Toolbars is disabled when there are no custom toolbars. An item does not repeat its label as a tooltip. A tooltip that adds something else is placed on that item and uses the dock colors. The customize button on a toolbar opens "Add or Remove Buttons". Every button with a stable key has a check item there; uncheck it to hide the button. While the toolbar is floating, the menu also has a checkable Vertical item. Reset undoes the button changes and puts that toolbar back on the edge, band, index, offset, and alignment declared on it. A floating toolbar docks there. Other toolbars in a shared window stay floating. Reset also clears a vertical float and restores one line. A hidden toolbar is shown. A custom toolbar also has Delete Toolbar next to Reset. A built-in toolbar does not. Delete asks first in a dialog styled like New Toolbar, then removes the toolbar. It works on a window tray, a pane tray, and a float. Deleting a floating toolbar closes its window. Alt+drag a button to reorder it, move it to another toolbar, or drop it outside the toolbars to hide it. Customization is saved per button key. The key is DockToolBar.Key if set. Otherwise it comes from ToolBarItemKeyPath, then the element's Name, ContentId, Id, or a string ToolTip or ToolTipText. A button with none of these gets a key for the current session only: its changes are not saved, and it doesn't appear in the customize menu. Give your buttons names or keys. Set ToolBarCustomizationEnabled to false to turn off Alt+drag, the customize menu, and the tray menu everywhere. Set IsCustomizable to false to do the same for one toolbar. By default the dock keeps the user's button order as an overlay and leaves your item collections alone. Set ToolBarMoveItemsInSource to true if a reorder or a move between toolbars should edit the source lists too. Only do that when those lists are writable. ToolBarCustomizationChanged fires after a button is reordered, moved, copied, removed, hidden, shown, or reset, and when a toolbar is created, renamed, deleted, shown, or hidden. ToolBarId names the toolbar. ItemKey is the button's key, or null when the change is about the toolbar itself. FromToolBarId is set when a button came from another toolbar. Custom toolbars The tray menu has New Toolbar. It asks for a name and floats an empty toolbar near the pointer. DockManager.CreateCustomToolBar does the same and floats it at (48, 48). The name is trimmed. An empty name, or a name another toolbar already uses, is rejected. Enter accepts the dialog and Escape cancels it. The dialog follows the dock theme, including a custom theme. Themes lists the brushes. Edit Custom Toolbars is the next item. It is disabled when there are no custom toolbars. The dialog lists every custom toolbar by name. Pick one and rename it, or delete it. Rename uses the same rule as New Toolbar: the name is trimmed, and an empty name or a name another toolbar already uses leaves the dialog open. Delete asks in the dialog before the toolbar is removed. Deleting a floating toolbar closes its window. The list, the text box, and the buttons use the same brushes as New Toolbar. When the last custom toolbar is deleted, the dialog says there are none. A custom toolbar is a ToolBarEntry with Custom, Title, and the copied button keys in Items. It has no host collection. The tray menu shows the name. A float shows it as the caption tooltip and the grip tooltip, not as caption text, including when the float is vertical. Right-click its caption or its grip to rename it or delete it. Delete removes that toolbar only. The buttons it copied stay on the toolbars they came from. Alt+drag onto a custom toolbar copies. The original stays where it is, still visible and enabled. The copy is a stand-in: clicking it clicks the original, and IsEnabled and Visibility follow the original. The stand-in keeps the original button's width and height. It uses the original style when that style's target type fits, and the toolbar's button style otherwise, so a float of copied icon buttons is the same size as the toolbar they came from. An Image or a Path is cloned, so the icon shows in both places. Any other visual is shown as text. Alt+drag inside the custom toolbar reorders the copies. Alt+drag a copy off it, or onto a normal toolbar, removes the copy and does not move the original. Alt+drag onto a normal toolbar still moves the button, and the original collapses there until that toolbar is reset. A plain drag does not move or copy a button. A separator can be copied the same way. The copy is a real separator. Dropping a separator onto a normal toolbar does not move it. The custom toolbar is in the tray menu with its own check mark. Add or Remove Buttons lists its copies, and unchecking one hides that copy, not the original. Reset clears the copies and leaves the toolbar where it is, including a float. Reset on a normal toolbar is unchanged. Delete Toolbar is the next item, and only on a custom toolbar. It asks before it removes the toolbar, whether that toolbar is docked, on a pane, or floating. Cancel leaves it. Deleting a float closes the window. RenameCustomToolBar and DeleteCustomToolBar are the same operations. SaveLayout writes custom, title, and items only when they are set, so an older file stays the same bytes. A custom toolbar with no title, or item ids that are empty or repeated, is rejected. A key whose button is missing at load stays in items and is shown again when that button exists. Layout persistence DockManager.SaveLayout writes bands, alignment, floating bounds, a vertical float, a shared float's floatId and floatIndex, visibility, button order, and custom toolbars to DockLayout.ToolBars, and LoadLayout restores them. custom, title, and items are left out when they are the default. floatVertical is left out when it is false. lines is left out when the toolbar is one line. floatId and floatIndex are left out when they are null and zero. A file without a toolBars object loads fine. See Saving and loading layouts.

articles/xaml.html.title: Working in XAML | SmartDock
articles/xaml.html.summary: Working in XAML You can declare the layout, toolbars, key bindings, and theme on the window itself. MarkupWindow does all of that, and its code-behind only calls InitializeComponent, which any window with x:Class needs. <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.MarkupWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" xmlns:local="clr-namespace:SmartDock.Docs.Samples" xmlns:model="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock.Core" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <Window.DataContext> <local:ThemeChoice /> </Window.DataContext> <Window.InputBindings> <KeyBinding Key="F" Modifiers="Control" Command="{x:Static dock:DockCommands.ToggleFloat}" CommandTarget="{Binding ElementName=Dock}" /> <KeyBinding Key="H" Modifiers="Control" Command="{x:Static dock:DockCommands.ToggleAutoHide}" CommandTarget="{Binding ElementName=Dock}" /> </Window.InputBindings> <dock:DockManager x:Name="Dock" local:SampleContent.Prepare="True" Theme="{Binding Theme}"> <dock:DockManager.ToolBars> <ToolBar dock:DockToolBar.Id="standard" dock:DockToolBar.Title="Standard" dock:DockToolBar.Edge="Top" dock:DockToolBar.Band="0" dock:DockToolBar.Alignment="End" dock:DockToolBar.PaneId="solution"> <Button dock:DockToolBar.Key="save" Content="Save" /> <Button Content="Float" Command="{x:Static dock:DockCommands.ToggleFloat}" CommandTarget="{Binding ElementName=Dock}" /> <Button Content="Blue" Command="{Binding UseBlue}" /> </ToolBar> </dock:DockManager.ToolBars> <dock:DockManager.Layout> <model:DockLayout> <model:DockLayout.Root> <model:SplitNode Id="root" Orientation="Horizontal"> <model:SplitNode.Children> <model:SplitChild Proportion="0.25"> <model:SplitChild.Node> <model:TabGroupNode Id="tools" Kind="Tool"> <model:TabGroupNode.Panels> <model:DockPane ContentId="solution" Title="Solution Explorer" Kind="Tool" CanClose="False" CanAutoHide="True" /> <model:DockPane ContentId="properties" Title="Properties" Kind="Tool" /> </model:TabGroupNode.Panels> </model:TabGroupNode> </model:SplitChild.Node> </model:SplitChild> <model:SplitChild Proportion="0.75"> <model:SplitChild.Node> <model:TabGroupNode Id="docs" Kind="Document"> <model:TabGroupNode.Panels> <model:DockPane ContentId="program" Title="Program.cs" /> <model:DockPane ContentId="readme" Title="README.md" /> </model:TabGroupNode.Panels> </model:TabGroupNode> </model:SplitChild.Node> </model:SplitChild> </model:SplitNode.Children> </model:SplitNode> </model:DockLayout.Root> </model:DockLayout> </dock:DockManager.Layout> </dock:DockManager> </Window> Layout The tree uses the same node types as Layout. A DockPane in XAML only names a content id. It doesn't create the control, and RegisterContent is a method, so markup can't call it. This sample works around that with local:SampleContent.Prepare, an attached property defined in LayoutWindow.xaml.cs. XAML sets it on the start tag, before the Layout property element, so the content factories are registered before the panes are created. Theme is bound to ThemeChoice, a small class with a DockThemeKind property. The manager repaints whenever that value changes. using System.ComponentModel; using System.Windows.Input; namespace SmartDock.Docs.Samples; public sealed class ThemeChoice : INotifyPropertyChanged { private DockThemeKind _theme = DockThemeKind.Light; public ThemeChoice() => UseBlue = new RelayCommand(_ => Theme = DockThemeKind.Blue); public DockThemeKind Theme { get => _theme; set { if (_theme == value) return; _theme = value; PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(nameof(Theme))); } } public ICommand UseBlue { get; } public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged; } The Blue button runs UseBlue, which sets Theme to Blue. Themes lists the three palettes. To change individual colors, put Dock.* brushes in DockManager.Resources. They win over the theme and reach floating windows, the guide overlay, the auto-hide flyout, and toolbar windows. A dictionary shared by several windows goes on DockManager.CustomTheme instead. Styling and templates lists the keys. Content from a collection If your items are the content, you don't need factories at all. DocumentsSource and ToolsSource take any IEnumerable. An item that is a UIElement becomes the pane body. Any other item is shown through DocumentTemplateSelector, then DocumentTemplate, then the implicit DataTemplate for its type. Tools use ToolTemplateSelector, ToolTemplate, and the same implicit lookup. The implicit template is found with TryFindResource on the manager, which checks the manager's own resources, then parents such as the window, then application resources. The lookup runs when the item is added and again when the manager gets a parent and when it loads, so the templates can live in Window.Resources, as they do in MarkupDocumentsWindow. A template you add after the manager has loaded isn't applied to items that are already open. A template that came from DocumentTemplate, ToolTemplate, or a selector is never replaced by this lookup. This window's code-behind also only calls InitializeComponent. <Window x:Class="SmartDock.Docs.Samples.MarkupDocumentsWindow" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml/presentation" xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml" xmlns:dock="clr-namespace:SmartDock;assembly=SmartDock" xmlns:local="clr-namespace:SmartDock.Docs.Samples" Title="SmartDock" Height="640" Width="960"> <Window.Resources> <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type local:MarkupDocument}"> <TextBox Text="{Binding Text, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" AcceptsReturn="True" BorderThickness="0" /> </DataTemplate> <DataTemplate DataType="{x:Type local:MarkupTool}"> <TextBlock Text="{Binding Text}" Margin="12" TextWrapping="Wrap" /> </DataTemplate> </Window.Resources> <dock:DockManager> <dock:DockManager.Resources> <Style x:Key="DocumentItem" TargetType="dock:DockItem"> <Setter Property="Title" Value="{Binding Title}" /> <Setter Property="ContentId" Value="{Binding ContentId}" /> <Setter Property="CanClose" Value="{Binding CanClose}" /> <Setter Property="CanFloat" Value="{Binding CanFloat}" /> </Style> <Style x:Key="ToolItem" TargetType="dock:DockItem"> <Setter Property="Title" Value="{Binding Title}" /> <Setter Property="ContentId" Value="{Binding ContentId}" /> <Setter Property="CanClose" Value="{Binding CanClose}" /> <Setter Property="CanFloat" Value="{Binding CanFloat}" /> <Setter Property="CanAutoHide" Value="{Binding CanAutoHide}" /> <Setter Property="HideOnClose" Value="{Binding HideOnClose}" /> </Style> </dock:DockManager.Resources> <dock:DockManager.DocumentItemStyle> <StaticResource ResourceKey="DocumentItem" /> </dock:DockManager.DocumentItemStyle> <dock:DockManager.ToolItemStyle> <StaticResource ResourceKey="ToolItem" /> </dock:DockManager.ToolItemStyle> <dock:DockManager.DocumentsSource> <x:Array Type="{x:Type local:MarkupDocument}"> <local:MarkupDocument ContentId="program" Title="Program.cs" Text="class Program" /> <local:MarkupDocument ContentId="readme" Title="README.md" Text="Notes" CanClose="False" /> </x:Array> </dock:DockManager.DocumentsSource> <dock:DockManager.ToolsSource> <x:Array Type="{x:Type local:MarkupTool}"> <local:MarkupTool ContentId="solution" Title="Solution Explorer" Text="Projects" CanClose="False" CanAutoHide="True" /> </x:Array> </dock:DockManager.ToolsSource> </dock:DockManager> </Window> DocumentItemStyle and ToolItemStyle target DockItem, with the source item as the data context. You can set Title, ContentId, Icon, CanClose, CanFloat, CanAutoHide, and HideOnClose. A pane with an empty title shows its content id instead. An empty ContentId is replaced with item- followed by eight hex digits. A saved layout finds an item again only when its id is the same string, so give items fixed ids if you save layouts. Icon isn't saved in the layout file. If a tool's style doesn't set CanAutoHide, it defaults to true, the same as DockTree.Tool. This window binds it, so the value comes from MarkupTool. MarkupDocument and MarkupTool are in MarkupDocument.cs. x:Array doesn't implement INotifyCollectionChanged, so adding to it later has no effect. Use an ObservableCollection when the list changes; MVVM shows how. The first pane added to an empty manager becomes the root. After that, a new document joins the main-tree document group that last held the active document. If there isn't one, it joins the first document group, and if there are no document groups, it goes to the right of the root at 0.75. A new tool joins the first tool group, or goes to the left of the root at DockEdit.DefaultProportion (0.25). An id that is already docked, floating, auto-hidden, or hidden stays where the layout put it. Toolbars The toolbar in MarkupWindow uses the DockToolBar attached properties. Edge, Band, Alignment, and PaneId only set where it starts. Once the toolbar has been shown or dragged, its saved position wins, and changing these properties doesn't move it. PaneId="solution" starts the toolbar on that pane, and an unknown pane id falls back to the main window's top tray. Toolbars lists the other attached properties. DockToolBar.Key on the Save button is the key that customization is saved under. A button with no key, Name, content id, or string tooltip gets a key that lasts only for the session. That key isn't saved, and the button doesn't appear in the customize menu. Commands DockCommands holds routed commands that the manager already handles: ClosePane, NextDocument, PreviousDocument, ToggleFloat, ToggleAutoHide, SaveLayout, and LoadLayout. The manager and each floating window have handlers for them. A button outside the manager needs CommandTarget set to the manager, because otherwise the command routes from wherever focus is and may never reach it. A button or menu item inside the manager can leave CommandTarget unset. ToggleFloat, ToggleAutoHide, SaveLayout, and LoadLayout have no default key, so the window adds Ctrl+F and Ctrl+H with key bindings. A KeyBinding adds a gesture without removing the defaults: ClosePane is still Ctrl+F4, NextDocument Ctrl+PageDown, and PreviousDocument Ctrl+PageUp. To change a default, replace the command's InputGestures. DockCommands is static, so the change applies to every manager in the process. See Keyboard. ToggleFloat floats the active pane at (80, 80), 480 by 360, if it's allowed to float, and docks a floating pane back. ToggleAutoHide does nothing when the active pane can't auto-hide, as with the Properties pane here, which leaves CanAutoHide false. SaveLayout writes the current layout to SavedLayout, which MVVM binds. LoadLayout reads that string and applies it again, which is how you restore a save after the user has moved panes. It does nothing when SavedLayout is null or empty. What still needs code RegisterContent can't be called from markup, and a DockPane in XAML doesn't create its control. Either call RegisterContent before Layout is assigned, or wrap it in an attached property the way SampleContent.Prepare does. If you'd rather avoid both, use DocumentsSource and ToolsSource, which don't need it. Next: MVVM.

index.html.title: SmartDock | SmartDock
index.html.summary: SmartDock SmartDock is a docking library for WPF on .NET 8. A layout is a tree of splits and tab groups. Every pane has a stable content id, and when a layout is shown or restored, the dock maps each id back to your control. There are two packages, both in the SmartDock namespace: SmartDock is the WPF part. DockManager draws the splits, tabs, floating windows, auto-hide strips, and toolbars. SmartDock.Core has the layout model, the edit operations, and the JSON serializer. It doesn't reference WPF, so a service or a command-line tool can build and save layouts too. Features Horizontal and vertical splits. Proportions are weights and do not have to sum to 1. Document and tool tab groups. Only the selected tab's content is in the visual tree. Dock a pane to the left, right, top, or bottom of an anchor, or add it as a tab. Floating windows with their own captions. They can be maximized and docked back. Auto-hide strips and flyouts for tool panes that allow it. Drag a tab along its strip to reorder it, or off the strip to float it, then drop it on a dock guide. Hide a pane and show it again later. A hidden pane stays in the saved layout. Save and load the whole layout as compact JSON, including floats, auto-hide, hidden panes, and toolbars. Toolbars on the main window and on panes, including a pane inside a floating window or an open auto-hide flyout, with a customize menu. Their positions are saved with the layout. They do not dock to the outside of a floating window. A Ctrl+Tab pane switcher, plus commands for close, document cycling, float, and auto-hide. Dark, light, and blue chrome. Dark is the default. Events for layout changes, closing, pane state, activation, and when a pane's content is mounted or unmounted. Bind documents and tools to a collection, with a data template per item. Install dotnet add package SmartDock --version 0.16.2 It pulls in SmartDock.Core. If you only build or store layouts, the core package is enough: dotnet add package SmartDock.Core --version 0.16.2 The WPF package needs net8.0-windows. SmartDock.Core targets plain net8.0. Read next Getting started Layout Working in XAML MVVM Saving and loading layouts Toolbars Keyboard Themes Styling and templates Events and callbacks API reference Issues Report bugs and API questions at https://github.com/ArcticNoise/SmartDock/issues.
